title: Partner centrality and alliance formation by peripheral firms
x: Potential partner network centrality conditional on focal firm having below-mean centrality
setting: A chemical-industry firm with below-mean alliance-network centrality considers a technical alliance. Its potential partner can have below-mean or at-least-mean centrality, measured consistently from the preceding four-year alliance network. Both firms must participate; centrality does not confer ownership or unilateral authority.
task: Rate how changing the prospective partner from low to high network centrality changes alliance-formation likelihood for the peripheral firm. Compare lower X (Both firms below annual mean centrality) with higher X (Focal firm below mean, potential partner at or above mean). Use the same X contrast in both contexts. A positive rating means higher X is associated with more Y; a negative rating means less Y. Rate the relationship, not the overall level of Y. Do not interpret this judgment as a measured empirical coefficient.

xContrast.lower: Both firms below annual mean centrality
xContrast.higher: Focal firm below mean, potential partner at or above mean

sharedFacts: The focal firm remains below mean centrality in both contexts.
Higher partner centrality means changing from a below-mean partner to an at-least-mean partner; combined dyad centrality is not artificially held fixed.

sourceEvidence.citation: Ahuja, G., Polidoro, F., Jr., and Mitchell, W. (2009). Structural Homophily or Social Asymmetry? The Formation of Alliances by Poorly Embedded Firms. Strategic Management Journal, 30(9), 941-958. doi:10.1002/smj.774.
sourceEvidence.measurementNotes: Chemical industry technical alliances; focal firm remains peripheral; identical centrality definition
sourceEvidence.translationNotes: Bonacich eigenvector centrality in symmetric prior-four-year alliance network; contrast also changes combined centrality. H2 weakens to p<0.07 controlling combined centrality. Do not substitute majority ownership H3.
